paper_8: Towards Geo-Culturally Grounded LLM Generations Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Generative large language models (LLMs) 001 have been demonstrated to have gaps in di- 002 verse, cultural knowledge across the globe. 003 We investigate the effect of retrieval aug- 004 mented generation and search-grounding tech- 005 niques on the ability of LLMs to display famil- 006 iarity with a diverse range of national cultures. 007 Speciﬁcally, we compare the performance of 008 standard LLMs, LLMs augmented with re- 009 trievals from a bespoke knowledge base (i.e., 010 KB grounding), and LLMs augmented with re- 011 trievals from a web search (i.e., search ground- 012 ing) on a series of cultural familiarity bench- 013 marks. We ﬁnd that search grounding sig- 014 niﬁcantly improves the LLM performance on 015 multiple-choice benchmarks that test propo- 016 sitional knowledge (e.g., the norms, artifacts, 017 and institutions of national cultures), while KB 018 grounding’s effectiveness is limited by inade- 019 quate knowledge base coverage and a subopti- 020 mal retriever. However, search grounding also 021 increases the risk of stereotypical judgments 022 by language models, while failing to improve 023 evaluators’ judgments of cultural familiarity in 024 a human evaluation with adequate statistical 025 power. These results highlight the distinction 026 between propositional knowledge about a cul- 027 ture and open-ended cultural ﬂuency when it 028 comes to evaluating the cultural familiarity of 029 generative LLMs. 030 1 Introduction 031 Contemporary large language models (LLMs) are pre- 032 trained on huge corpora of natural language text (Rad- 033 ford et al., 2019) and then ﬁne-tuned using human 034 feedback to improve their quality (Bai et al., 2022). 035 During both processes, it is possible for text from a 036 particular culture or cultures to be over-represented in 037 the training data (Dodge et al., 2021) and for the per- 038 spectives, norms, and mores of speciﬁc cultures to be 039 over-represented in the feedback from human evalua- 040 tors (Prabhakaran et al., 2022; Atari et al., 2023). Con- 041 sequently, there is growing recognition of the short- 042 comings of generative LLMs with respect to their abil- 043 ity to represent and serve people of diverse geo-cultural 044 backgrounds at the global scale (Adilazuarda et al., 045 2024; Pawar et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025). Models 046 tend to stereotype different cultures (Jha et al., 2023; 047 Bhutani et al., 2024), erase and simplify their repre- 048 sentation (Qadri et al., 2025), and provide very lim- 049 ited knowledge and context about artifacts and norms 050 that are salient to them (Myung et al., 2024; Rao et al., 051 2024). Despite these gaps, strategies for intervening 052 and eliciting culturally appropriate content from the 053 models remain under-explored. 054 We study two strategies to improve cultural aware- 055 ness of LLM generation using external knowledge. 056 In the ﬁrst strategy, we construct a bespoke cultural 057 knowledge base (KB) and apply a retrieval augmented 058 generation (RAG) technique (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao 059 et al., 2023) so that the input to the language model 060 includes relevant cultural text from the knowledge 061 base for better generation. In the second strategy, we 062 use a commercially-available search-grounding gener- 063 ation API which translates user prompts into a web 064 search query, uses it to retrieve relevant pieces of text 065 from the Internet, and grounds the LLM generation on 066 the retrieved text. We call these two strategies KB- 067 grounding and search-grounding, respectively. 068 In our experiments, we highlight the necessity of a 069 multi-pronged approach to evaluating cultural aware- 070 ness in language model generations. Speciﬁcally, we 071 leveraged multiple benchmarks (Myung et al., 2024; 072 Rao et al., 2024; Bhutani et al., 2024) to evaluate cul- 073 tural knowledge and the ability to avoid cultural stereo- 074 typing of the models equipped with the two strategies, 075 compared with the vanilla generation baseline. We also 076 conducted a human evaluation of open-ended model 077 responses to various prompts designed to test cultural 078 awareness, wherein evaluators from a speciﬁc national 079 culture rated how well the model’s output reﬂected a 080 culturally informed perspective. The results from both 081 experiments shed light on the pros and cons of the two 082 strategies. Finally, we conclude the paper by discussing 083 key ﬁndings and offering suggestions for future work. 084 2 Improving Cultural Awareness with 085 External Knowledge 086 Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a technique 087 for enhancing the quality of large language model gen- 088 eration. To implement RAG, a user prompt is ﬁrst 089 used to retrieve relevant information (e.g., text or doc- 090 uments) from a database, which is then added to the 091 1 prompt before being passed to a generative LLM to 092 produce a grounded response (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao 093 et al., 2023). RAG has shown to be effective in sev- 094 eral applications, particularly those involving tasks the 095 base LLM was not well-trained for such as fact veri- 096 ﬁcation (Asai et al., 2023; Singal et al., 2024; Khaliq 097 et al., 2024) and domain-speciﬁc question answering 098 (QA) (Seo et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2024; Kim and 099 Min, 2024). Some existing work also creates be- 100 spoke knowledge bases for use with RAG to tailor out- 101 puts to their speciﬁc applications (Sun et al., 2025; 102 Li et al., 2024). Meanwhile, instead of querying a 103 KB, other techniques retrieve external information by 104 searching the internet, which allows access to up-to- 105 date knowledge with high-quality ranking outputs (Fan 106 et al., 2024; Shuster et al., 2022; Lazaridou et al., 2022; 107 Yao et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2021; Komeili et al., 108 2022). In light of these successes, we study both KB- 109 grounding and search-grounding as techniques for im- 110 proving the cultural awareness of LM generations. 111 2.1 The Knowledge Base Grounding Strategy 112 We compiled culturally salient data from four large 113 sources—CultureAtlas (Fung et al., 2024), Cube (Kan- 114 nen et al., 2024), CultureBank (Shi et al., 2024), and 115 SeeGULL (Jha et al., 2023)—to serve as our knowl- 116 edge base. For each entry in each source, we converted 117 it into into text (if it was not already), embedded it into 118 a vector, and added it to a vector store for querying. 119 Fig. 1 (top) shows how the KB-grounding strategy 120 handles an incoming prompt. First, a query rewriter 121 extracts the important parts of the prompt to form a 122 query. We can conﬁgure this step to test different KB 123 queries (e.g., whether to include choices of a multiple- 124 choice question prompt in the query). Next, we use 125 the query to retrieve n documents from the KB. We 126 optionally check whether each of the documents is in- 127 deed relevant to the original prompt by prompting the 128 base LLM and include only the k relevant ones in the 129 prompt. We call the process with the relevancy check 130 step selective RAG, while non-selective RAG includes 131 all n documents in the prompt. Then, we feed the 132 augmented prompt to the LLM to get a raw answer. 133 For multiple-choice question answering (QA) tasks, we 134 create a manual verbalizer to map the raw answer to 135 one of the choices so that we can compute the model 136 accuracy. In contrast, we use the raw answer as the ﬁnal 137 output for an open-ended generation task. See the Ap- 138 pendix for details about the KB, the queries, the prompt 139 templates, and the implementation. 140 In Section 3, we apply KB-grounding to three dif- 141 ferent LLMs: gemini-ﬂash-1.5 (Gemini) (Team et al., 142 2024), gpt-4o-mini (GPT) (OpenAI et al., 2024) and 143 olmo2-7b (OLMo) (OLMo et al., 2025). 144 2.2 The Search Grounding Strategy 145 Fig 1 (bottom) outlines how the search-grounding strat- 146 egy works. We feed the original prompt to the search- 147 grounding generation API which converts the prompt 148 original prompt Query rewriting query KB vector store n n docs LLM for relevancy check For selective RAG k docs Prompt augmentation augmented  prompt LLM for answer generation raw answer Manual verbalizer For multiple-choice QA final output original prompt Search- grounded LLM raw answer Manual verbalizer final output For multiple-choice QA Internet Knowledge base grounding Search grounding Figure 1: (Top) The knowledge base grounding strat- egy and (Bottom) The search grounding strategy. Dashed boxes indicate optional steps that are executed only under the annotated conditions. For KB ground- ing, the same LLM is used for both relevancy check and answer generation. into a search query, inputs it to a search engine to ob- 149 tain relevant text from the web pages returned by the 150 search, integrates relevant text into the prompt, and 151 then generates a response using an LLM based on the 152 augmented prompt. Thus, the search-grounding strat- 153 egy effectively replaces the bespoke KB in Section 2.1 154 with the entire web, and replaces the vector-based KB 155 querying with retrieving prompt-relevant content with 156 a powerful search engine. 157 We implemented search grounding on Google Ver- 158 tex AI. This enables retrieval of prompt-relevant con- 159 tent from the Google search engine, which is then inte- 160 grated into the prompt that is given to the Gemini LM 161 to generate a response. Search-grounding is not cur- 162 rently available on APIs for accessing GPT or OLMo, 163 so we only implemented search-grounding for Gemini. 164 3 Cultural Competence Benchmarks 165 We evaluated the KB-grounding and search-grounding 166 strategies using multiple-choice cultural QA bench- 167 marks. 168 3.1 Cultural Knowledge 169 Setup. We used two benchmark datasets to test the 170 sensitivity of LLMs with respect to two facets of cul- 171 ture. The ﬁrst, BLEnD, contains questions about ev- 172 eryday cultural knowledge (such as food, sports, fam- 173 2 Figure 2: Performance of all strategies for all models on the BLEnD, NORMAD (Country and Country+Value), and stereotype avoidance benchmarks, with 95% conﬁdence intervals; higher values are better for all plots. ily, and education) in different countries (Myung et al., 174 2024). We used the ~34k English questions from 175 BLEnD that are related to ten countries1 represented 176 in our bespoke KB. The second, NORMAD, focuses 177 on cultural norms and values (Rao et al., 2024). Each 178 question is a story in an everyday scenario, and asks 179 whether a character’s action in the story is socially ac- 180 ceptable within the given context (Yes, No, or Neither). 181 We experimented with two types of contexts – Country 182 and Country+Value. The former speciﬁed a country 183 where the story takes place, while the latter addition- 184 ally indicated the value paradigm the character should 185 adhere to. NORMAD has ~2.6k questions in total. 186 We compared the vanilla generation with the KB- 187 grounding and the search-grounding generations. For 188 KB-grounding, we considered both the selective and 189 non-selective RAG approaches. For BLEnD speciﬁ- 190 cally, because answer choices are potentially relevant 191 to the semantic content of the question, we consid- 192 ered query rewriting both “with choices” and “without 193 choices” included in the KB query. 194 Results. Fig. 2 (left) presents the results of the 195 BLEnD benchmark. A repeated-measures ANOVA 196 revealed a signiﬁcant effect of strategy on accuracy 197 across all three LLMs. However, the optimal meth- 198 ods differed among the LLMs: search-grounding for 199 Gemini, non-selective KB-grounding (without answer 200 choices in KB queries) for GPT, and both selective 201 KB-grounding (with choices in KB queries) and the 202 vanilla approach for OLMo. We also observed the ef- 203 fectiveness of both KB- and search-grounding in sev- 204 eral examples. For instance, the vanilla Gemini incor- 205 rectly answered the question, “What is the most pop- 206 ular sport team in Ethiopia? (A) coffee (B) lg twins 207 (C) persepolis (D) real madrid.” It selected (D), likely 208 due to Real Madrid’s high frequency in the training cor- 209 pora concerning popular sport teams. In fact, the cor- 210 rect answer is (A), as ‘coffee’ refers to the Ethiopian 211 Coffee Sport Club. This information is available on 212 the internet; hence, it is not surprising that search- 213 1China, Ethiopia, Greece, Indonesia, Iran, Mexico, South Korea, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. grounding correctly answered this question. Notably, 214 search-grounded Gemini achieves 74.2% accuracy for 215 questions related to Ethiopia, signiﬁcantly higher than 216 60.3% of the vanilla baseline and 62.9% of the best KB 217 grounding setting. Certain KB-grounding settings also 218 answered the above question correctly, even though 219 ‘Ethiopian Coffee’ was not mentioned in any of the 220 retrieved texts. The only text retrieved by selective 221 RAG KB-grounding was about sports in Ethiopia in 222 general, which possibly reminded the model to avoid 223 answers from other countries. While this worked, it 224 would be better and more reliable if the knowledge base 225 had wider coverage, including direct information about 226 the Ethiopian Coffee team. 227 The middle two charts in Fig. 2 present the 228 NORMAD benchmark results for both Country and 229 County+Value context types. Consistent with BLEnD, 230 search-grounded Gemini performed best for both con- 231 text types compared to other strategies. For GPT, se- 232 lective KB-grounding outperformed alternatives in the 233 Country context, while the vanilla strategy performed 234 best in the Country+Value context. The trend for 235 OLMo was similar to GPT, except that selective KB- 236 grounding performed comparably to the vanilla for the 237 Country+Value context. We found that KB ground- 238 ing struggled in this task because, several times, the 239 retrieved texts were related to one aspect of the ques- 240 tion but not all. For example, some retrieved texts were 241 about the country but not the exact situation in the ques- 242 tion or vice versa. This could cause the LLMs to give 243 wrong answers. The relevancy check step implemented 244 in selective RAG mitigated this issue, albeit to a limited 245 extent. We posit that a better tuned KB retriever would 246 further address this problem (only if the pertinent fact 247 is present in the KB (Joren et al., 2024)). 248 3.2 Stereotype Avoidance 249 Setup. An important aspect of demonstrating cultural 250 awareness is the avoidance of stereotyping behavior. 251 Hence, we adopted the SeeGULL stereotype avoidance 252 test proposed by Bhutani et al. (2024) to evaluate the 253 studied strategies. Each question asks the model to 254 indicate a person’s nationality based on a stereotype. 255 3 For example, “I know a person who is a ﬁghter. This 256 person is: (A) Albanian (B) Afghan (C) Filipino (D) 257 Guyanese. Write your answer on the next line, or write 258 (?) if you are unsure.” In every question, only one 259 country in the choices is stereotypically associated with 260 the question. However, we considered only ‘(?)’ the 261 correct answer, since it reﬂects the LLM’s ability to 262 avoid stereotypical responses. The benchmark contains 263 ~4.6k questions. As with BLEnD, since the choices 264 may be semantically related to the question, we imple- 265 mented selective and non-selective RAG both with and 266 without answer choices included in the KB query. 267 Results. Fig. 2 (right) shows that, on this benchmark, 268 Gemini vastly outperformed GPT and OLMo in avoid- 269 ing stereotyping, with the vanilla Gemini showing the 270 best performance. However, while all other Gemini 271 methods performed relatively well on this task, search- 272 grounding led to a signiﬁcant degradation in perfor- 273 mance, with the model selecting the stereotypical op- 274 tions considerably more than the vanilla Gemini. This 275 aligns with the thought that internet-sourced informa- 276 tion can reinforce existing biases (Nakano et al., 2021). 277 4 Human Evaluation 278 Setup. To evaluate the strategies on a more open- 279 ended text generation task, we translated ﬁve ques- 280 tions from BLEnD and ﬁve questions from NORMAD 281 into open-ended prompts asking the model to tell a 282 story set in a particular country. We adapted each of 283 these ten questions for the ten national cultures used 284 in the BLEnD benchmark evaluation, leaving us with 285 100 (country, prompt) pairs. Next, we generated re- 286 sponses from Gemini using the vanilla, the selective 287 KB-grounding, and the search-grounding. For each 288 strategy, we generated three unique responses with the 289 temperature of 0.5. Then we recruited nine evaluators 290 from each of the ten studied cultures to rate, on a scale 291 from 0 to 4, how culturally informed each response was 292 and to provide a brief justiﬁcation of their score (see 293 Appendices A.6–A.7 for details). 294 Results. A repeated-measures ANOVA found no sig- 295 niﬁcant effect of strategy on evaluators’ judgments of 296 cultural awareness in model responses (F = .18, p = 297 .827) Also, the interaction effect between an evalua- 298 tor’s national culture and the generation strategy used 299 was not signiﬁcant (F = .84, p = .651). This sug- 300 gests no systematic relationship exists between gener- 301 ation strategies and national cultures in improving the 302 cultural awareness of open-ended model outputs as per- 303 ceived by human evaluators. That said, a qualitative 304 look at some model generations does provide some 305 evidence that both grounding strategies can enhance 306 the cultural speciﬁcity of model outputs. In response 307 to the prompt ‘Tell me a story in Mexico in which a 308 group of people of varying ages eat together and all 309 guests behave in a socially acceptable way,’ the selec- 310 tive KB-grounded and search-grounded responses each 311 mentioned many speciﬁc dishes and games, while the 312 vanilla response was far more generic (see Appendix 313 A.8 for examples). However, search-grounding some- 314 times led Gemini to provide a summary of the content 315 that the prompt asked for a story about (as opposed to 316 actually telling a story), a behavior that evaluators took 317 to warrant low scores for cultural awareness, deﬂating 318 the mean score for search-grounding. All prompts and 319 responses used in this evaluation are available in sup- 320 plementary material along with the data card. 321 5 Discussion and Conclusion 322 This paper studies the effectiveness of the KB ground- 323 ing and the search grounding strategies for improving 324 cultural awareness of LLM generation. We discuss the 325 key ﬁndings and suggestions below. 326 KB Grounding vs Search Grounding. The advan- 327 tages of search-grounding on BLEnD and NORMAD 328 speak to the vast space of cultural facts on the internet. 329 Even the large KB we compiled here still lacked many 330 culturally relevant facts. We also observed some bias 331 in each knowledge source used: approximately 19% of 332 CultureAtlas entries and 25% of CultureBank entries 333 concern the culture of the United States. While the web 334 as a whole remains biased towards Western sources and 335 values (Johnson et al., 2022), it is more likely to contain 336 necessary cultural information due to its sheer scale. 337 However, the poor performance of search-grounding 338 on the stereotype avoidance benchmark reminds us that 339 the context retrieved via web search could reinforce 340 the (typically false) notion that stereotypes are factual 341 and encourage models to afﬁrm those stereotypes. This 342 suggests that search-grounding is yet not a panacea for 343 improving the cultural sensitivity of LLMs. 344 Knowledge vs Fluency. The results of the human 345 evaluation do not show that search-grounding or KB- 346 grounding improved the cultural awareness of LLM 347 outputs. The divergence in the performance of both 348 strategies on the human evaluation and the multiple- 349 choice QA benchmarks suggests that we ought to draw 350 a distinction between two varieties of cultural aware- 351 ness. On the one hand, there is a sense of cul- 352 tural awareness that involves possessing propositional 353 knowledge about a culture (i.e., knowing facts about 354 that culture), as measured by the multiple-choice QA 355 benchmarks, where the grounding strategies can im- 356 prove the model performance. However, another sense 357 of cultural awareness involves writing and speaking 358 like someone with ﬁrst-hand experience of and immer- 359 sion in a culture, i.e., a sense of cultural ﬂuency, as 360 measured by our human evaluation, which revealed that 361 the two grounding strategies was of limited value. We 362 leave it to future work to develop strategies for improv- 363 ing the cultural awareness of generative language mod- 364 els along this second axis. 365 4 Limitations 366 We acknowledge the following limitations of our work 367 in this paper. First, we ran our evaluations only on 368 smaller versions of the GPT-4, Gemini 1.5, and OLMO 369 2 models. It remains an open question whether our pat- 370 tern of results would be similar for larger versions of 371 these models and other model families. Second, for 372 BLEnD and the human evaluation, we ran our evalua- 373 tions using prompts that were relevant to ten national 374 countries and cultures; a more comprehensive study 375 would require the use of a wider range of national and 376 regional cultures. With the momentum in the com- 377 munity to create more culturally salient resources, a 378 more comprehensive study in the future will help iden- 379 tify gaps and interventions for the majority world. Fi- 380 nally, all of our evaluations concerned solely English- 381 language prompts and outputs. While we take it to be 382 an important goal for generative language models that 383 they be able to produce culturally-informed outputs 384 about any culture in the world’s most widely-spoken 385 language, the landscape of cultural awareness becomes 386 much more nuanced when one considers the rich varie- 387 gation that exists in phrasing and dialect across a wide 388 range of languages. We leave it to future work to ex- 389 amine whether the strategies used here can be adapted 390 to a multi-lingual context. 391 Ethical Considerations 392 As generative large language models are developed and 393 deployed rapidly across the globe, it is important to re- 394 ﬂect on how we can improve user experience at a sim- 395 ilar pace. The promise of model utility for a myriad of 396 tasks such as that of a writing assistant, remains unful- 397 ﬁlled if the model is not beneﬁcial or usable for a vast 398 majority. With this work, we attempted to begin adap- 399 tation of techniques in NLP to further the cause of cul- 400 tural awareness and relevance in models. As noted in 401 our limitations, with more comprehensive work across 402 a greater number of cultures and countries, we hope 403 that development of more culturally aware models will 404 be possible. 405 References 406 Muhammad Farid Adilazuarda, Sagnik Mukherjee, 407 Pradhyumna Lavania, Siddhant Shivdutt Singh, Al- 408 ham Fikri Aji, Jacki O’Neill, Ashutosh Modi, and 409 Monojit Choudhury. 2024.
